newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: European cocoa trade slack as bulk arrives.
newsitem.headline: European cocoa trade slack as bulk arrives.

text.p: Cocoa traders in continental Europe said on Friday ship arrivals from the Ivory Coast were progressing smoothly, if a little late, but that physical trading had begun to wind down ahead of the Christmas period.
"If there is something offered afloat, it is being bought directly by one of the main processors," one trader said.
"At this time of year the demand is pretty low."
Butter ratios were described as steady at around 2.70 for the first quarter 1997 and 2.65 for the rest of the year.
Sterling's continued strength was another factor behind lacklustre offtake from industry, they added.
London-traded cocoa futures fell on Friday, the benchmark March contract dropping nine stg to 923, in a move described by traders as purely technical.

The market has shown little reaction to a crop projection from a senior Ivorian diplomat that the country's cocoa production in the 1996/97 season would come in at between 850,000 and 900,000 tonnes, including the mid-crop.
"That figure looked very low. History shows the Ivorian crop is usually bigger than originally thought," one trader said.
Traders said they were sticking to their earlier projections of a total crop of just above one million tonnes.
But they also noted that arrivals in Abidjan were lower than last year and that the latest Ghanaian purchases were also down.
"Arrivals may be later but there's enough cocoa," one said.
Bulk shipments had already begun to arrive in Amsterdam, and more were due soon, carrying cargoes of 3,500 to 5,000 tonnes.
"This is very much an experimental year as regards bulk shipments but it has produced a big change in the market," one trade source added.
According to the latest estimates from SGS Warehouse Services, stored beans in Amsterdam totalled 415,000 tonnes at the start of the month, up 5,000 tonnes from a month earlier.
